notes.meaning: Sheba, a troublemaker from the tribe of Benjamin, took advantage of an argument between the tribes. He blew a ram's horn and shouted that the northern tribes had no share in King David. By calling David the son of Jesse, he insulted the king and urged everyone to abandon him.

The northern tribes turned away from David and chose to follow Sheba instead. In contrast, the men of Judah remained loyal and walked with David from the Jordan River to Jerusalem. Even when a crowd walks away, true loyalty stands firm.

David returned to his palace in Jerusalem and dealt with the ten concubines he had left behind. Because Absalom had publicly violated them, David did not live with them as wives again, but he did not mistreat them. He housed, guarded, and provided for them as widows for the rest of their lives.

David ordered Amasa to call together the army of Judah within three days and report back in person. The king had promised Amasa the top military position to replace Joab and win over former rebels. David wanted to crush the new rebellion quickly before it could grow.

Amasa went out to gather the soldiers of Judah, but he missed the three-day deadline. The people may have hesitated to follow him because he had led Absalom's rebel army earlier, or he struggled to organize them in time. His delay left the kingdom in serious danger.

David realized that Sheba could cause even more harm than Absalom if he took shelter inside walled cities. Because Amasa was late, David did not wait. He passed over Joab and ordered Joab's brother Abishai to take the royal guard and chase Sheba down immediately.

Abishai marched out of Jerusalem with David's royal bodyguards, elite warriors, and the soldiers who usually served under Joab. Joab went with them as well, looking for a way to regain his command. The army rushed out to stop Sheba before he could fortify himself.

Amasa caught up with the troops at the great stone near Gibeon and stepped forward to lead them. Joab wore his military coat with a belt holding a dagger in its sheath. As Joab walked forward, the blade slipped out so he could hold it in his hand without raising suspicion.

Joab greeted Amasa warmly like a brother and asked about his health. He took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss his cheek, which was a customary friendly greeting. This polite act completely disarmed Amasa and hid Joab's cruel plan.

Amasa did not notice the blade ready in Joab's left hand. Joab stabbed him in the belly with a single blow and killed him instantly. Joab and his brother Abishai then hurried off to pursue Sheba, leaving Amasa on the ground.

One of Joab's young men remained standing by Amasa's body to give orders to the approaching soldiers. He shouted that anyone who supported Joab and David should follow Joab. By joining Joab's name with the king's name, he persuaded the troops to keep moving.

Amasa lay dying in his own blood in the middle of the road. The passing soldiers stopped in shock and could not take their eyes off their fallen commander. Seeing that the gruesome sight blocked the whole army, the young man dragged the body into a field and covered it with a cloth.

As soon as the body was out of sight, the soldiers stopped hesitating and marched forward. They followed Joab to chase down Sheba and put an end to the revolt. Removing the distraction allowed the troops to focus on their mission.

Sheba fled north through all the tribes of Israel, trying to stir up a wider revolt. He finally took refuge in Abel-beth-maacah, a fortified town near the northern border, along with his relatives. Joab and his army tracked him all the way to that distant city.

Joab's army surrounded the city and piled up a dirt ramp against the outer wall. From this ramp, the soldiers could attack the defenses directly and batter the wall to bring it down. The entire town faced sudden ruin because it harbored a rebel.

A wise woman called out from the city wall to get the attention of the attackers. She asked the soldiers to fetch Joab so she could speak with him directly. Her courage opened a path to peace before any more lives were lost.

Joab walked over to the wall, and the woman made sure she was speaking to the commanding general. When he confirmed who he was, she asked him to listen to what she had to say. Joab agreed to listen, showing that he was willing to hear reason.

The woman reminded Joab of an old saying that people should seek counsel at Abel to resolve hard disputes. The city had a long reputation for wisdom and fair settlements. She suggested that Joab should have talked with the city before bringing war against it.

The woman spoke on behalf of her town, stating that the citizens were peaceful and loyal to Israel's king. She called Abel a mother in Israel, meaning an important city that nurtured and protected the surrounding villages. She asked Joab why he would destroy land that belonged to the Lord.
Joab answered that he had no desire to swallow up or destroy an innocent town. He strongly denied that he came to ruin the Lord's people. He wanted only to capture the man who had caused the trouble.

Joab explained that Sheba had rebelled against King David and hidden inside the city. He promised to withdraw his army immediately if the townspeople handed over that one man. The woman agreed and promised that Sheba's head would be thrown over the wall.

The woman took her wise plan to the citizens, and they agreed to cut off Sheba's head and toss it over the wall to Joab. Joab blew the horn to sound the retreat, and the soldiers dispersed back to their homes. Joab then returned to King David in Jerusalem with the rebellion ended.

Joab was established once again as commander over the entire army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada served as the leader of the Cherethites and Pelethites, the king's trusted bodyguards. Although Joab had murdered Amasa to reclaim his rank, David lacked the power to remove him.

Adoram supervised the kingdom's forced labor force and tax collections. Jehoshaphat served as the royal recorder, keeping track of state events and legal documents. This list shows that the royal government was running in an orderly way again after the civil war.

Sheva served as the king's royal scribe, handling official letters and records. Zadok and Abiathar continued in their duties as priests leading the nation in worship before God. The king relied on organized leadership to maintain peace across the land.

Ira the Jairite was appointed as a priest or chief personal adviser to David. While the official priests led worship for the nation, Ira served as a trusted spiritual counselor directly in David's court. Even a great king needed wise spiritual support in his daily life.
